# Letter of Jeremiah Chapter 1 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Letter of Jeremiah 1 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/LJR_001_page_001.jpg

---

**1** This is a copy of the letter Jeremiah sent to the exiles being marched to Babylon by the Babylonian king — a message he was commanded by God to deliver.

**2** Because of the sins you committed against God, you are going to Babylon as prisoners of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.

**3** Once you arrive, you will stay there for many long years — through seven generations, in fact. After that, I will bring you out in peace.

**4** In Babylon you will see gods of silver, gold, and wood being carried on people's shoulders, filling the nations with dread.

**5** Watch yourselves. Do not become like those foreigners, do not let terror of those gods take hold of you

**6** when you see the crowds pressing in from every side to worship them. Say in your own hearts: "You alone deserve worship, Lord."

**7** My own messenger is with you, and he is the guardian of your lives.

**8** Their tongues have been smoothed by the craftsman's hand. They are plated with gold and silver. But they are frauds — they cannot speak a word.

**9** They are like a young woman who loves jewels, crowning her head with gold —

**10** while the priests pocket the gold they strip from their gods, spending it on themselves, or tossing some to the prostitutes on the roof.

**11** They dress up these silver, gold, and wooden gods like human beings —

**12** yet those same gods cannot protect themselves from rust and moth. The priests drape purple robes over them

**13** and then have to wipe the dust off their faces — dust that piles thick in the temple.

**14** One of them is propped up like a governor with a scepter, as though he rules over criminals —

**15** yet he cannot bring a single wrongdoer to justice. He holds a sword and an axe in his hand, but he cannot save himself from war or thieves.

**16** This makes it perfectly clear they are not gods. Do not be afraid of them.

**17** Just as a clay pot becomes worthless once it breaks, so it is with their gods. Set up in houses, their eyes fill with dust from the feet of everyone who walks in.

**18** Just as a courtroom is locked tight against a condemned criminal, so the priests bar and bolt their temple doors against robbers.

**19** Lamps burn before them — more lamps than the priests burn for themselves — yet the gods cannot see a single one.

**20** They are no better than one of the wooden beams in the roof. The story goes that their hearts are eaten away by creatures that crawl from the floor — worms devour them and their clothing, and they feel nothing.

**21** Their faces are blackened by the smoke that fills the house.

**22** Bats, swallows, and every sort of bird land on their bodies and their heads. Cats do the same.

**23** From this you can see plainly they are not gods. Do not be afraid of them.

**24** That gold plating, put on for beauty — unless someone polishes away the tarnish, it will not shine. And when they were being cast in the mold, they felt nothing.

**25** They were bought at enormous cost. But there is no breath in them.

**26** They have no feet. They are carried on people's shoulders, parading their own disgrace in front of everyone. Are not even their servants ashamed?

**27** If one falls to the ground, it cannot get up by itself. If someone props it up, it cannot stand on its own. Offerings placed before them are placed before the dead.

**28** The priests sell off the sacrifices and keep the money. Their wives cure some of the meat for themselves. But the poor and the helpless? They get nothing.

**29** Women who are unclean — even menstruating women — handle their sacrificial offerings. This alone should make it clear: these are not gods. Do not be afraid of them.

**30** How can these things be called gods, when women place the food-offerings before silver and gold and wooden statues?

**31** In their temples the priests sit with torn robes, their heads shaved, their beards shaved, their heads bare.

**32** They wail and cry before their gods the way people do at a funeral.

**33** The priests take the robes right off the gods and put them on their own wives and children.

**34** Do good to these gods or harm them — they cannot respond either way. They cannot make a king or remove one.

**35** They cannot give wealth or money. If someone makes a vow and does not keep it, they cannot collect. They will never come looking for what was promised.

**36** They cannot pull a man back from death. They cannot protect the weak from the powerful.

**37** A blind man? They cannot restore his sight. A man in desperate need? They cannot come to his aid.

**38** They will not take pity on a widow. They will do nothing for an orphan.

**39** Their wooden and stone and gold and silver gods are like rocks on a mountainside. Those who worship them will end up in disgrace.

**40** So how can anyone in their right mind believe or say that they are gods?

**41** Even the Chaldeans themselves have no real respect for them. When they hear of a mute man who cannot speak, they drag out Bel and demand that he speak for the man — as though Bel could hear or understand anything.

**42** They cannot figure this out and give these gods up, because they have no capacity for understanding.

**43** Women sit along the roads with cords tied around them, burning stalks of grain.

**44** And whenever some passing man pulls one of them aside and sleeps with her, she mocks the woman sitting next to her, sneering that she herself was chosen and her cord was broken, while the other woman was not.

**45** Everything connected with these gods is a lie. How can anyone really believe or say that they are gods?

**46** They are put together by carpenters and goldsmiths. They will be nothing more or less than whatever the craftsmen decide to make them.

**47** And the craftsmen who made them? They will not live long themselves. So how can things they made be gods?

**48** They leave nothing to future generations but lies and disgrace.

**49** When war or disaster strikes, the priests huddle together deciding where to run — taking their gods with them to hide.

**50** Can anyone still fail to see that these things are not gods? They cannot even save themselves from war or catastrophe.

**51** They are nothing but wood covered in gold and silver. One day the whole world will know they are frauds. Every nation, every king will see plainly: they are not gods, they are objects made by human hands, and there is no trace of God's work in them.

**52** Who could doubt, looking at them, that they are not gods but human craftsmanship, with not a trace of God's work in them?

**53** They cannot raise up a king over a country. They cannot send rain.

**54** They cannot settle a legal dispute. They cannot free a country from oppression. They are powerless — like crows flapping between heaven and earth.

**55** When fire breaks out in a temple housing these wooden and silver and golden gods, the priests run for their lives — but the gods get burned like timbers in the blaze.

**56** They cannot face a king in battle. How can anyone possibly accept that they are gods?

**57** Wooden and stone and gold and silver gods cannot protect themselves from burglars and looters.

**58** Any strong man can strip away their gold and silver, take their clothing, and walk off. The gods cannot lift a finger to stop him.

**59** Better, then, is a righteous king than a useless idol. Better, too, is a clay pot that actually serves its owner than false gods.

**60** Better are the doors of a house that actually protect what is inside. Better even is a wooden post in a palace.

**61** The sun, the moon, the stars — they blaze with light, they serve real purposes, they obey.

**62** Lightning flashes and you can see it. Wind blows through every country.

**63** Clouds, when God sends them rolling across the whole earth, do exactly what they are told. Fire sent down from on high to burn mountains and forests carries out its orders.

**64** Not one of these can be compared to the idols — not in appearance, not in power.

**65** The conclusion is clear: such things are not to be thought or called gods. They can neither judge nor do good for human beings.

**66** Since you now know they are not gods, do not be afraid of them.

**67** They cannot curse kings. They cannot bless them.

**68** They show no signs in the sky to the nations. They do not shine like the sun. They do not give light like the moon.

**69** Animals are better than they are — animals can run to cover and save themselves.

**70** So it is completely plain to us that they are not gods. Do not be afraid of them.

**71** They are like a scarecrow in a cucumber field — it guards nothing. So are their wooden and golden and silver gods.

**72** They are like a wild-thorn bush in a garden that every bird perches on. Or like a dead body tossed out into the dark.

**73** The purple and linen rotting on their backs will tell you everything: they are not gods. In the end they themselves will be eaten away and become a byword of shame in the land.

**74** Better, then, is a righteous man who owns no idols — for he will never have to face that shame.
